results.title: Navigating the Family-Wise Error Rate (FWER)
results.content: Navigating the Family-Wise Error Rate (FWER): Insights, Methods, and Real-World Applications By clicking Continue to join or sign in, you agree to LinkedIn’s User Agreement, Privacy Policy, and Cookie Policy. Navigating the Family-Wise Error Rate (FWER): Insights, Methods, and Real-World Applications ### DEBASISH DEB In today's data-driven landscape, statistical testing is the backbone of decision-making across industries. The Family-Wise Error Rate (FWER) is a statistical concept that addresses this challenge by controlling the likelihood of making at least one false positive error across a set of hypothesis tests. This article delves into the FWER, its assumptions, methods for control, and real-world applications, ensuring you gain a comprehensive understanding of its significance and practical use. The FWER quantifies the probability of making at least one Type I error across a family of hypothesis tests. Independence or Positive Dependency: Most methods assume the tests are independent or positively correlated. ### Methods to Control FWER Several approaches exist to control FWER, each with its trade-offs between stringency and statistical power: ### 1. * Limitation: Overly conservative, especially with a large number of tests, reducing statistical power. An improvement over the Bonferroni correction, this stepwise method ranks p-values and compares them sequentially with adjusted thresholds: * Advantage: More powerful than Bonferroni while still controlling FWER. A less conservative alternative to Bonferroni, it assumes independence among tests: * Advantage: Retains slightly higher power under independence assumptions. An enhancement of Holm-Bonferroni, Hochberg’s method adjusts p-values in descending order and is more powerful: * Advantage: Controls FWER effectively while retaining greater power. ### Bonferroni Correction: A Double-Edged Sword ### Impact on Study Power: While effective at controlling FWER, Bonferroni correction significantly reduces the power of a study, especially with small effect sizes or large test counts. ### Handling Different Tests: Bonferroni is agnostic to the type of test but becomes less effective with dependent tests, where methods like Westfall-Young may be preferred. ### Conclusion The Family-Wise Error Rate is a cornerstone of sound statistical analysis, ensuring robust conclusions in the face of multiple testing. Whether in clinical trials, genomics, or business analytics, selecting the right method to control FWER is key to balancing precision and power.

results.title: On selecting the critical boundary functions in group-sequential trials with two time-to-event outcomes - ScienceDirect
results.content: ## Article preview. ## Contemporary Clinical Trials. # On selecting the critical boundary functions in group-sequential trials with two time-to-event outcomes. We investigate selection of critical boundary functions for testing the hypotheses of two time-to-event outcomes as both primary endpoints or a primary and a secondary endpoint in group-sequential clinical trials, where (1) the effect sizes of endpoints are unequal, or (2) one endpoint is for short-term evaluation and the other for long-term evaluation. We investigate combinations of critical boundary functions for testing the hypotheses associated with two time-to-event outcomes as both primary endpoints, or a primary and a secondary endpoint, in group-sequential clinical trials, which can maximize the power of rejecting either or both of the null hypotheses associated with the two endpoints. They assumed that the statistical information fraction for each endpoint is the same at a particular time-point of analysis and the trial is terminated when the null hypothesis of the primary endpoint is rejected regardless of whether the null hypothesis of the secondary endpoint is rejected. We consider the two multiple testing procedures, Bonferroni-Holm (BH) and fixed-sequence (FS) procedures, which are commonly used in clinical trials. ## A group-sequential clinical trial with time-to-event endpoints. We discussed the selection of critical boundary functions for testing the hypotheses associated with two time-to-event outcomes as both primary endpoints, or a primary and a secondary endpoint, in group-sequential clinical trials, where (1) the effect sizes of the two endpoints are unequal, or (2) one endpoint represents short-term evaluation and the other long-term evaluation. ## References (19). * D.M.
